chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Ibn Udhaynah from Zurarah who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the 'jirith', so he said, 'And what is the jirith?' So I described it to him, and he said, 'I do not find in what was revealed to me that it is forbidden for a consumer to consume it,' until the end of the verse.

Then he said, 'God did not forbid anything from animals in the Quran except the pig itself, and it is disliked (makruh) of everything from the sea that has no shell, like the 'wariq', and it is not forbidden (haram), it is merely disliked.'

key_terms.الْجِرِّيثُ: A specific type of sea creature mentioned in the hadith
key_terms.الْخِنْزِيرَ: The pig, the only animal explicitly forbidden in the Quran
key_terms.الْوَرِقِ: A type of shellfish or sea creature without a hard shell
key_terms.مَكْرُوهٌ: Disliked or recommended to avoid, but not forbidden

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating sea creatures without shells in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) distinguishes between explicit Quranic prohibitions, citing the pig as the sole animal explicitly named as haram, and other sea creatures which are deemed makruh (disliked) rather than strictly haram. This hadith highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that in the absence of a specific textual prohibition, the default status of food is permissibility, with 'makruh' indicating a recommended avoidance rather than a binding prohibition.
